final: Who settled a dispute changed across our history: first the teachers, then the bishop, and at the end the council. Early on, teachers argued with books, lectures, and letters, and authority went to proven wisdom. In the middle years the bishop's judgment grew, and Demetrius condemned Origen's ordination. At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the disputed confession for all, and the emperor who called the council backed the council with force. The rule of faith, the short summary of what the apostles handed down, set the bounds within which inquiry into Scripture could range. After Nicaea, the bishop of Alexandria became the enforcer of conciliar orthodoxy across Egypt, with exile, letter-networks, and synods as the bishop's tools. Our best picture of deciding well is Bishop Dionysius's own account of his work with the village churches. The village churches near Arsinoe loved a bishop named Nepos. He had written a book against the allegorists. The promises in Scripture, he said, meant a thousand-year kingdom of plenty on this earth, plainly read. Nepos had died, and his book now ruled whole congregations. That book is lost. We know it only from the bishop who answered it. Our bishop Dionysius went out to the villages. He told the story himself, in his book On the Promises, and Eusebius later quoted it. He called together the elders and the teachers, and any of the people who wished to come. For three days, from morning to evening, he sat with them and examined the book, argument by argument. He wrote afterward that he loved Nepos for his faith, his hard work in the Scriptures and his psalms. Even so, he wrote, "the truth should be loved and honored most of all." He rejoiced in the constancy and sincerity of the believers, and in their willingness to reconsider as they weighed the arguments together. At the end, Coracion, the leader of the other side, was persuaded. He said so in front of everyone. Some of the other believers, the account says, were glad at the spirit of agreement all had shown. The arguments exchanged in the villages survive only in Dionysius's summary, and Nepos's book is lost, known only through the man who refuted Nepos's book.

judgement.reason: It is evidence for one bishop settling one dispute by open argument, not for the whole teacher-bishop-council process.

question: When your people disagreed about doctrine, who settled it, and what evidence tells us that process actually worked that way?
